2.2a — Spikes: Collisions, Health & Death

Coins were a ghost passing through a wall; spikes are a wall. Same meeting, different physics — and today you also meet the death loop: the most consequential six lines in the starter project.

Predict First ~10 min

Read the spike half of PlayerController.cs:

private void OnCollisionEnter2D(Collision2D collision)
{
    if (collision.gameObject.CompareTag("Spikes"))
    {
        if (StatManager.manager != null)
        {
            StatManager.manager.ChangeHealth(-1);
        }
    }
}

Notice what changed vs yesterday: a different method (OnCollisionEnter2D, not OnTriggerEnter2D), a different parameter type (Collision2D, not Collider2D), and — this is the part to predict — the coin vanishes when you touch it, but the spikes do NOT destroy you. You slide off them. What is different about the Spikes prefab's collider that makes Unity call a collision instead of a trigger?

Then find the answer in the Inspector: select the Spikes prefab and look at its BoxCollider2D — Is Trigger is unchecked. Same component, one checkbox, two different events.

The rule, once and forever: a trigger lets things pass through (coins, pickups, ladders — "touching means something"); a solid collider stops things (spikes, walls, floors — "bumping means something"). If your handler never fires, check which checkbox the collider has before touching a single line of code.
Build Lab ~20 min

Step 1 — rebuild the damage. Comment out the spike branch and retype it: collide → tag → ChangeHealth(-1). Run: watch the Console count 3 → 2 as you bump spikes. Then die on purpose.

Step 2 — read the death loop. In StatManager.cs:

public void ChangeHealth(int amount)
{
    health += amount;
    Debug.Log("Health Changed! New Health: " + health);

    if (health <= 0)
    {
        Debug.Log("Player Died!");
        HandleDeath();
    }
}

private void HandleDeath()
{
    // Halve coins rounded down
    coins = Mathf.FloorToInt(coins / 2f);
    health = 3;
    UnityEngine.SceneManagement.SceneManager.LoadScene("Start");
}

Trace the consequence chain out loud: spike → ChangeHealth(-1) → health 0 → HandleDeath → coins cut in half (rounded down), health restored, scene reset. Death has a cost — half your coins. That is game design: not a game-over screen, a tax.

Step 3 — where does health live? Select the StatManager object in the Hierarchy and watch the Inspector while you spike yourself: health ticks 3 → 2 → 1 in the Inspector — live, in play mode. The number you see is the number ChangeHealth mutates.

Bug Hunt: Hurt yourself on purpose

  1. What happens when you land on two spike tiles at once? One −1 or several? Why does the answer depend on how the tiles are built?
  2. Change the spikes' collider to Is Trigger. What breaks — and which method would you have to switch to in order to fix it?
  3. Set starting health to 1 in the StatManager's Inspector. How fast is death now — and is 1 too punishing for the Overworld? Argue one sentence.
  4. In HandleDeath, comment out the LoadScene line. What happens at zero health instead — and what did the scene reset actually protect you from?
Tinker ~15 min

Tinker: Design the damage

  1. Spikes cost 1 heart. Design a trap that costs 2 — what changes in code, what changes in the scene, and where would a new tag go?
  2. Death halves your coins. Why "rounded down" — what would 1 coin halve into, and what does FloorToInt(0.5) actually produce?
  3. Hard mode: a spike tile that only hurts if you touch the TOP of it. Could a single if-statement inside OnCollisionEnter2D do it? (Hint: collision knows more than the tag — explore what it carries.)

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Say when Unity calls OnTriggerEnter2D vs OnCollisionEnter2D — and why
  • Walk through the death loop line by line: health, coins, scene
  • Explain why death is a coin tax instead of a game-over
  • Check a collider's Is Trigger box before blaming the code
